title: Y'Fei Nof
program_note:
Yehuda HaLevi, born around 1075 in Toledo, Spain, was a famed philosopher and physician, but is better known as one of the very greatest Jewish poets of all time.  Many of his poems speak of his longing—and the longing of the Jewish people—for the ancient capital of Jerusalem.  He left Spain in 1140 (at the age of 65), with the intention of visiting Jerusalem, after a stop in Alexandria, Egypt.  Legend has it that he died in 1141, trampled by a horseman at the gates of Jerusalem.
One of his best known poems is “Y’fey Nof” (“Beautiful View,” “Beautiful Vista,” or “Beautiful Prospect”), in which HaLevi’s passion for Jerusalem is palpable:

יְפֵה נוֹף מְשׂוֹשׂ תֵּבֵל קִרְיָה לְמֶלֶךְ רָב / לָךְ נִכְסְפָה נַפְשִׁי מִפַּאֲתֵי מַעְרָב
הֲמוֹן רַחֲמַי נִכְמָר כִּי אֶזְכְּרָה קֶדֶם / כְּבוֹדֵךְ אֲשֶׁר גָּלָה וְנָוֵךְ אֲשֶׁר חָרָב
וּמִי יִתְּנֵנִי עַל כַּנְפֵי נְשָׁרִים, עַד / אֲרַוֶּה בְדִמְעָתִי עֲפָרֵך וְיִתְעָרָב
דְּרַשְׁתִּיךְ, וְאִם מַלְכֵּךְ אֵין בָּךְ וְאִם בִּמְקוֹם / צְרִי גִּלְעֲדֵך - נָחָשׁ שָׂרָף וְגַם עַקְרָב
הֲלֹא אֶת אֲבָנַיִךְ אֲחוֹנֵן וְאֶשָּׁקֵם / וְטַעַם רְגָבַיִךְ לְפִי מִדְּבַשׁ יֶעְרָב

Beautiful prospect, joy of the world, city of a great king,
For you yearns my spirit, from the farthermost edge of the west.

My compassion overflows within me, remembering when
Your honor was revealed to all, before the city was scorched.

And who will give to me, with which to fly to you, eagle’s wings,
until, with all of my gathered tears, I drench your parchèd soil?

I seek you, and if your king is not within you, and in place
of Balm of Gilead a fiery serpent and scorpion,

Yet even so, onto your stones will I plant many kisses,
and the taste of your soil will be as if mixed with honey.
Translation by David S. Lefkowitz

HaLevi was quite attentive to rhyme, rhythm, meter, and feet in his poetry.  Y’fey Nof features a set meter for the entire poem, with nearly the exact same number of syllables and metrical feet in every line.  The musical setting maintains that metrical structure, highlighted by the clapping lines.  (The translation above is intended to respect the number of syllables of the Hebrew original, but not the exact metrical structure:  metrically better substitutions for the word “beautiful,” for instance, would be “attractive” or “appealing,” yet neither of those two words convey quite the right sense.)

David S. Lefkowitz
12 August, 2024
Los Angeles, CA
